name: Fintech & Markets
description: Terms to be fluent in for Bloom content, creator briefs, and the Finance Cheat Sheet. Register: a good Gen Z finance script — accurate, plain, never condescending.

entries.definition: One hundredth of a percentage point — the unit finance uses when “percent” is too clumsy to be precise.
examples: When a fund says it charges 75 basis points, it means 0.75% a year, every year, whether you made money or not.
Script note: say “bps” out loud as “bips” and immediately translate it, or half the audience tunes out.
The Fed cut 25 basis points and every finance account on the app posted about it within the hour.
conversation: Viewer comment: what does 75 bps even mean
You: Basis points. Seventy-five of them is 0.75 percent a year, every year, whether the fund makes you money or not.
entries.note: Exists because “a 1% cut from 5%” is ambiguous — is that to 4% or to 4.95%? Basis points remove the ambiguity, which is why fees are quoted in them.

entries.definition: How fast something can be turned into cash without losing value in the process.
synonyms: how fast you can cash out
examples: Every “finance guru” on TikTok says liquidity like it's magic — it just means how fast you can turn a thing into cash without losing value.
Your checking account is perfectly liquid. Your sneakers are not, and the resale market will remind you at the worst possible time.
A stock can be liquid and still be a bad investment; liquidity is about exit speed, not quality.
conversation: Friend: My sneakers are worth like eight hundred.
You: On paper. Can you get eight hundred by Friday? That is liquidity, and it is the whole difference.
entries.note: Best script framing: the question isn't “is it worth $500,” it's “can I get $500 for it by Friday.” That's the whole concept.

entries.definition: Describing an account or service where someone else holds and safeguards the assets on your behalf.
examples: A custodial account is how a 16-year-old invests legally — an adult holds it, the kid owns it, and it transfers at 18 or 21 depending on the state.
In crypto, custodial means the platform holds your keys; non-custodial means you do, along with all the responsibility.
“Not your keys, not your coins” is a slogan about custody, and it cuts both ways.
conversation: Viewer: I am sixteen, can I even invest?
You: Through a custodial account. An adult holds it, you own it, and it transfers to you at eighteen or twenty-one depending on the state.
entries.note: Two contexts, one idea: someone is holding the thing for you. Always answer the follow-up — what happens if that someone fails?

entries.definition: Someone legally required to act in your interest ahead of their own.
examples: Ask any advisor one question: are you a fiduciary? If the answer takes more than a word, it's no.
A fiduciary has to recommend the cheaper fund when it's better for you; a salesperson only has to recommend something suitable.
The word is boring and it's the single highest-value question in the whole Finance Cheat Sheet.
conversation: Friend: My uncle knows a financial guy.
You: Ask him one question. Are you a fiduciary? If the answer takes longer than a word, it is a no.
entries.note: The best 15 seconds in any advice-adjacent script. It converts a fuzzy trust question into a specific legal one the audience can actually ask.

entries.definition: The annual percentage a fund takes out of your money to run itself, deducted automatically whether the fund goes up or down.
examples: A 1% expense ratio doesn't sound like anything until you run it over 30 years and it's eaten roughly a quarter of your ending balance.
Two funds tracking the same index at 0.03% and 0.60% are the same product at twenty times the price.
You never see the expense ratio leave your account, which is exactly why it works so well.
conversation: Viewer: Two funds, same index. Why is one better?
You: Expense ratio. 0.03 percent versus 0.60. Same product, twenty times the price, taken automatically either way.
entries.note: The most script-friendly number in personal finance because the comparison is so stark and requires no market opinion at all.

entries.definition: Investing a fixed amount on a fixed schedule regardless of price, so you buy more shares when it's cheap and fewer when it's expensive.
examples: $50 every payday is dollar-cost averaging, and its real benefit is that it removes the decision — you can't panic about timing something automatic.
DCA doesn't beat investing everything at once on average; it beats what you'd actually do with a lump sum at 2am.
The strategy is boring by design; that's the feature everyone tries to optimize away.
conversation: Friend: Should I wait for a dip?
You: Dollar-cost average instead. Fifty every payday. It will not beat perfect timing, but it beats what you would actually do at 2am.
entries.note: Be honest in scripts: lump-sum wins more often historically. DCA wins behaviorally, and behavior is what actually determines returns.

entries.definition: The schedule by which equity you've been promised actually becomes yours over time.
examples: Your offer says 10,000 shares, but vesting means you own zero until the one-year cliff and then a slice each month for three more years.
Leaving two months before your cliff means leaving with nothing, and it happens constantly.
Read the vesting schedule before the headline equity number — the schedule is the actual offer.
conversation: Friend: The offer says ten thousand shares.
You: Check the vesting. You own none until the one-year cliff, then a slice each month for three more years.
entries.note: The most under-explained line in every job offer, and a reliably high-performing content topic for anyone in their first real role.

entries.definition: The shrinking of your ownership percentage when new shares are issued to someone else.
examples: Every funding round dilutes existing shareholders — your 1% becomes 0.8% and the hope is that the smaller slice is of a much bigger pie.
Dilution isn't theft; it's the price of capital. It only stings when the round doesn't grow the pie.
Employees discover dilution at the exit, which is the worst possible time to learn about it.
conversation: Friend: They raised again. Is my equity worth less?
You: Your percentage is. That is dilution. A smaller slice of a bigger pie is fine — as long as the round actually grew the pie.
entries.note: Frame it as slice versus pie in scripts. The concept lands instantly and the number stops feeling like a trick.

entries.definition: Describing a long-term trend that runs across market cycles rather than with them.
examples: The shift of financial advice from institutions to individual creators is secular, not a 2021 bubble — it hasn't reversed through two market moods.
Don't confuse a secular trend with a cyclical bounce; one survives a recession and one is caused by the last one.
Secular trends are boring, slow, and where most of the money is.
conversation: Jae: Is creator-led finance a bubble?
You: Secular, not cyclical. It has survived two market moods and has not reversed once.
entries.note: Nothing to do with religion here. It's the finance sense — “across eras.” Pairs directly against cyclical, and the pair is a good memo structure.

entries.definition: Rising and falling with the broader economy in a repeating pattern.
synonyms: up and down with the cycle
examples: Trading app downloads are cyclical — they spike with volatility and evaporate in a quiet market, which makes our forecast a market call in disguise.
Luxury and travel are cyclical; utilities and groceries mostly aren't.
Calling a cyclical downturn a structural decline is how good companies get sold too cheap.
conversation: Jae: Why are you cautious about the Q1 forecast?
You: Downloads are cyclical. They spike with volatility and vanish in a quiet market. That forecast is a market call in disguise.
entries.note: For Bloom specifically, worth saying in a memo: how much of our growth is cyclical, and what does the number look like in a flat market?

entries.definition: Adding to value rather than subtracting from it — usually said of a deal that improves per-share earnings.
examples: The partnership is accretive on day one: their audience, our product, no new headcount.
An acquisition is accretive if the thing you bought earns more than the cost of buying it — anything else is a story about synergies.
Accretive is the finance word for “this made the pie bigger per person,” and it's the opposite of dilutive.
conversation: Jae: Is the partnership worth doing?
You: Accretive from day one. Their audience, our product, no new headcount.
entries.note: Sits in direct opposition to dilutive. Useful in a partnership memo, where it makes a fuzzy “good for both sides” claim into a testable one.

entries.definition: The original amount put in or borrowed, before any interest or returns.
examples: On a loan, early payments barely touch the principal — you're mostly paying interest, which is why the balance seems frozen for two years.
“Don't risk your principal” means don't gamble the money you actually need back.
Principal is the amount; interest is the rent on it.
conversation: Friend: I have paid this loan for two years and the balance barely moved.
You: Early payments mostly cover interest. Almost none of it touches the principal until later.
entries.note: Spelling matters and people get it wrong constantly: principal is money, principle is a rule. In captions, that error costs credibility fast.

entries.definition: The income something pays out over a year, expressed as a percentage of its price.
examples: A savings account at 4.5% yield pays you $45 a year on $1,000 — that's yield, and it's separate from whether the asset itself gained value.
High yield almost always means high risk; the market rarely hands out free income.
When a stock's price falls and the dividend doesn't, the yield goes up — which looks like good news and often isn't.
conversation: Viewer: The yield went up. Good news?
You: Careful. Yield rises when the price falls. Same payout, cheaper asset — that is often bad news wearing good numbers.
entries.note: The mechanical relationship — price down, yield up — is the single most confusing thing for beginners, and explaining it well is a great 45-second script.

entries.definition: How much and how fast a price swings around — the size of the moves, not their direction.
examples: Volatility isn't loss. It's the price of admission for returns that beat a savings account, and you pay it in stomach lining.
High volatility means a wide range of outcomes, which cuts both ways — people forget the upside half when they're scared.
Our install volume is correlated with market volatility, which is a nice tailwind and a terrible thing to build a forecast on.
conversation: Friend: I am down eleven percent, should I get out?
You: That is volatility, not loss. You only lose when you sell. The question is whether you can sit through it.
entries.note: The most valuable reframe in beginner content: volatility is a description of movement, not a synonym for danger. Losing money permanently is the risk.

entries.definition: Taking the position most of the market currently rejects, on the belief that the consensus is wrong.
examples: The contrarian take on finance content is that nobody wants more information — they want permission to start.
Being contrarian isn't a strategy on its own; you also have to be right, which is the part nobody posts about.
Contrarian and correct is where the returns are. Contrarian and wrong is most of the internet.
conversation: Maya: What is the contrarian angle for the post?
You: That nobody wants more information. They want permission to start. Contrarian and right, hopefully — contrarian alone is just a personality.
entries.note: The two-word test before publishing a contrarian post: contrarian and right, or just contrarian? The second is a personality, not an argument.

entries.definition: The economy-wide forces — rates, inflation, employment — that move everything at once regardless of individual quality.
examples: Don't build a script around macro; by the time it's edited, the Fed has moved and the video is wrong.
Macro explains why everything fell on Tuesday; it can't tell you which company was worth owning.
Half our Q1 lift was macro — rate-cut chatter pulled a lot of first-time investors into the market.
conversation: Creator: Should I do a video on the Fed?
You: Careful with macro. By the time you edit it, the Fed has moved and the video is wrong.
entries.note: Its opposite here is idiosyncratic — the stuff specific to one company. Separating the two is most of what sounding informed consists of.

entries.definition: Spreading money across things that don't move together, so no single bad outcome takes you out.
examples: Owning ten tech stocks isn't diversification; it's one bet with ten tickers.
Diversification is the only thing in finance that reduces risk without reducing expected return — that's why it gets called the free lunch.
Real diversification feels bad by design: something in the portfolio should always be underperforming.
conversation: Friend: I own ten tech stocks. That is diversified, right?
You: That is one bet with ten tickers. Diversification means owning things that do not move together.
entries.note: The emotional truth is the good script angle — a properly diversified portfolio always has a piece you resent, and that piece is doing its job.

entries.definition: A fund that mechanically buys everything in a defined list of companies instead of trying to pick winners.
examples: An index fund isn't a stock pick, it's a decision to stop picking — you buy the whole list and pay almost nothing for the privilege.
Most active funds lose to the index over ten years, and the ones that win rarely win twice.
The index fund is the most boring product in finance and the correct default for almost everyone starting out.
conversation: Viewer: Which stock should I pick first?
You: An index fund is a decision to stop picking. You buy the whole list and pay almost nothing for it.
entries.note: Careful in scripts: this is education, not advice. Explain what the thing is and how it works, and let the audience make the call.

entries.definition: The drop from a peak to the low that follows — how far down you went before recovering.
examples: A 50% drawdown needs a 100% gain to get back to even, and that asymmetry is the whole reason risk tolerance matters.
Before you pick an allocation, ask what drawdown you'd hold through without selling — that's your real risk tolerance, not the number in the quiz.
Every backtest looks great until you sit through its worst drawdown in real time.
conversation: Friend: I can handle risk.
You: Different question. What drawdown could you hold through without selling? Fifty percent down needs a hundred percent gain to get back.
entries.note: More useful than volatility for beginner scripts because it's a felt experience: this is how much of your money disappeared, and for how long.

entries.definition: A sustained decline of roughly 20% or more from a recent high.
examples: Bear markets happen about every six years, last around a year, and are the entire reason “time in the market” is a sentence people say.
The first bear market you invest through teaches you more about yourself than any risk quiz.
Our download volume falls in a bear market while our education content performs better — worth planning content around, not just reacting to.
conversation: Viewer: Everyone says we are in a bear market.
You: Twenty percent off the high, and it usually lasts about a year. It happens roughly every six.
entries.note: The 20% threshold is a convention, not a law. In scripts, give the number so the term stops sounding like weather.

entries.definition: A drop of about 10% from a recent high — smaller and far more frequent than a bear market.
examples: Corrections happen roughly once a year; treating each one as the beginning of a collapse is how people end up selling at the bottom.
The word itself is a bit of finance PR — it implies the previous price was a mistake being fixed.
A correction is a headline event and usually a non-event for anyone with a ten-year horizon.
conversation: Friend: Market is down eight percent, is this the crash?
You: Not yet. Ten percent is a correction and happens about once a year. Twenty is a bear market.
entries.note: Pair with bear market when explaining scale: 10% is a correction, 20% is a bear. Two numbers, and the audience has a working vocabulary.

entries.definition: The profit made when you sell something for more than you paid — and the thing that gets taxed.
examples: You don't owe capital gains tax because your portfolio went up; you owe it when you sell, which is why selling is a tax decision, not just a market one.
Hold longer than a year in the US and the gain is usually taxed at a lower long-term rate.
Nobody's first investing lesson mentions taxes, and then April arrives.
conversation: Friend: Do I owe tax because my portfolio is up?
You: Not until you sell. Then it is capital gains, and holding over a year usually means a lower rate.
entries.note: The realized-versus-unrealized distinction is the whole lesson. It's also the most common gap in otherwise decent finance content.

entries.definition: What you originally paid for an investment, used to work out your gain or loss when you sell.
examples: If you bought in three times at different prices, your cost basis is the blended average — and the app should show it, not make you do arithmetic.
A high cost basis means a smaller taxable gain, which is why tracking it matters more than people expect.
Transferring between brokerages can lose your cost basis history, and reconstructing it is genuinely miserable.
conversation: Friend: I bought in three times at different prices.
You: Then your cost basis is the blend. The app should show it, not make you do the maths at tax time.
entries.note: Good product-content overlap: showing cost basis clearly is a real UX advantage and worth a script explaining why the number is there.

entries.definition: How your money is split across different types of assets.
examples: Your allocation is the actual decision — which specific fund you picked matters much less than whether you're 90% stocks or 40%.
A 22-year-old and a 62-year-old should not have the same allocation, and neither should copy their favorite creator's.
Allocation first, product second; most beginner content does it backwards.
conversation: Viewer: Which fund is best?
You: Wrong first question. Your allocation matters more — ninety percent stocks versus forty is a bigger decision than which fund.
entries.note: The research is consistent that allocation drives most of the variation in returns. It's also the least exciting thing to make content about — the challenge, not a reason to skip it.

entries.definition: To sell some of what's grown and buy what's lagged, returning to your target mix.
examples: Rebalancing forces you to sell high and buy low on a schedule, which is the opposite of what you'd do on instinct.
If stocks ran and you're now 85% equities against a 70% target, rebalancing is maintenance, not a market call.
Once a year is plenty; rebalancing weekly is a hobby with a tax bill.
conversation: Friend: Stocks ran, so now I am at eighty-five percent equities.
You: Rebalance back to seventy. It forces you to sell high and buy low on a schedule, which is the opposite of instinct.
entries.note: The strongest emotional angle: it's a rule that makes you do the right thing at the exact moment you least want to. That's the script.

entries.definition: How long until you need the money — the input that determines what risk is reasonable.
examples: Money you need in 18 months for a deposit doesn't belong in the market, no matter how good the setup looks. That's a time horizon problem, not a conviction problem.
A 40-year horizon turns a bear market from a catastrophe into a sale.
Ask about the time horizon before the risk tolerance; one is a fact, the other is a mood.
conversation: Friend: Should I put my deposit money in the market?
You: When do you need it? Eighteen months is a time horizon problem, not a conviction problem. That money stays in cash.
entries.note: The single best question for any “what should I invest in?” comment, and it makes a great recurring script format.

entries.definition: How much loss you can actually sit through without selling — measured in behavior, not in intentions.
synonyms: how much loss you can sit through
examples: Everyone has a high risk tolerance in a bull market; you find out the real number the first time your account is down 30%.
Risk tolerance and risk capacity are different: one is how you feel, the other is whether you can afford it.
Build the portfolio for the version of you that's scared, not the one filling out the questionnaire.
conversation: Viewer: I have a high risk tolerance.
You: Everyone does in a bull market. You find the real number the first time you are down thirty percent.
entries.note: The honest framing for Gen Z content — self-knowledge outperforms optimization here, and that's a more useful message than another allocation chart.

entries.definition: The steady loss of purchasing power as prices rise — the same money buying less each year.
examples: Cash “feels” safe and loses about 3% of its buying power a year to inflation. Safe from volatility isn't the same as safe.
At 3% inflation, prices roughly double every 24 years, which is the entire argument for investing at all.
A 4% raise in a 5% inflation year is a pay cut wearing a nice email.
conversation: Friend: My money is safe in savings.
You: Safe from volatility, not from inflation. Three percent a year is a quiet three percent pay cut.
entries.note: The rule of 72 pairs perfectly here — divide 72 by the rate to get the doubling time. It's the most shareable piece of math in personal finance.

entries.definition: Stated at face value, before adjusting for inflation.
examples: That 7% is a nominal return; after inflation you kept about 4%, and the gap is where most “I'm doing great” stories live.
Nominal wages went up, real wages didn't, and everybody's confused about why the vibes are bad.
Any long-run number quoted without saying nominal or real is missing the most important word in the sentence.
conversation: Viewer: My account is up seven percent.
You: Nominal seven. Take three off for inflation and you actually kept four.
entries.note: Also means “trivially small” in everyday English (“a nominal fee”), which is a genuinely confusing overlap. In finance, always the face-value sense.

entries.definition: Adjusted for inflation — what the number is actually worth in purchasing power.
examples: Your savings account pays 4.5% nominal; with inflation at 3%, the real return is 1.5%, and that's the only number that buys anything.
Historical stock market returns are about 10% nominal and 7% real, and the second figure is the honest one to put in a script.
Real returns are what you eat; nominal returns are what you post.
conversation: Friend: Savings pays 4.5 percent, that is great.
You: Real return is about 1.5 after inflation. Still positive, just not the number on the poster.
entries.note: Teaching the nominal/real pair in one 30-second video is one of the highest-value things a finance creator can do. Most audiences have never had it named.

entries.definition: Ownership — the share of a thing that's actually yours after everything owed against it.
examples: Equity means ownership: a stock is a slice of a company, and startup equity is the same idea with worse liquidity and better upside.
You have $30K of equity in the car and a $22K loan, which means the bank still owns a real chunk of it.
Equity compensation is a bet on the company that you're paid in instead of cash.
conversation: Friend: What does equity actually mean?
You: The part that is yours after what is owed. A stock is a slice of a company. Home equity is the house minus the mortgage.
entries.note: Three overlapping senses — stocks, home equity, startup equity — and they're all the same underlying idea: what's left over that belongs to you.

entries.definition: A share of a company's profits paid out in cash to shareholders, usually every quarter.
examples: Dividends feel like free money and aren't — the share price drops by roughly the payout on the day it's paid.
A company that pays a dividend is telling you it has more cash than it has ideas, which isn't automatically bad.
Dividend investing is popular with beginners because the payment is visible and the compounding is legible.
conversation: Viewer: Dividends are free money, right?
You: Not quite. The share price drops by roughly the payout on the day. It is your own money handed back with a tax bill.
entries.note: Correcting the “free money” intuition without being condescending is a real craft challenge, and the videos that manage it perform.

entries.definition: What the market currently says something is worth — an opinion expressed as a price, not a measurement.
synonyms: what the market says it is worth
examples: A valuation isn't a fact about a company, it's the price at which the last buyer and seller agreed to stop arguing.
Startup valuations are negotiated on a story about the future; public valuations are negotiated on a story plus quarterly proof.
Two companies with identical revenue can have valuations 10x apart, and the difference is entirely belief about what happens next.
conversation: Friend: How can that startup be worth a billion?
You: A valuation is not a fact. It is the price at which the last buyer and seller stopped arguing.
entries.note: Great script framing: price is what someone paid, value is what it's worth, valuation is a crowd's guess at the second expressed as the first.

entries.definition: The total value of a company's shares — share price times number of shares.
examples: Share price alone tells you nothing: a $5 stock and a $500 stock can be the same size company with different share counts. Market cap is the actual size.
This is why “it's only $3, it could easily go to $300” is a red-flag sentence in any comment section.
Market cap sorts the universe into small, mid, and large — a more useful first cut than sector.
conversation: Viewer: It is only three dollars, it could easily hit three hundred.
You: Look at market cap, not share price. A three dollar stock and a five hundred dollar stock can be the same size company.
entries.note: The cheap-stock fallacy is one of the most common beginner mistakes, and market cap is the one-sentence cure. High-performing script topic.

entries.definition: How long a company can keep operating on the cash it has before it needs more.
synonyms: time before the money runs out
examples: Eleven months of runway means every budget conversation is really a conversation about the raise.
Runway is cash divided by net burn, and the number changes the moment you hire.
Knowing the runway is what separates a growth plan from a wish list.
conversation: You: Before I ask for budget — what is runway?
Jae: Eleven months.
You: Then this is really a conversation about the raise, and I will write it that way.
entries.note: Worth Jun knowing precisely, because a marketing budget request lands completely differently at 24 months of runway than at 9.

entries.definition: The cash a company spends beyond what it brings in, per month.
examples: Net burn is $400K a month, so every $100K of creator retainers is a week of runway — that's the honest way to frame the ask.
Gross burn is everything going out; net burn is what's left after revenue comes in.
Burn is the metric that turns strategy debates into arithmetic.
conversation: Jae: Frame the ask in something I feel.
You: Net burn is four hundred a month, so every hundred thousand in retainers is a week of runway.
entries.note: Always specify gross or net. Quoting the wrong one in a memo to a CEO is a small error that reads as not knowing the business.

entries.definition: Buying something purely because you expect its price to rise, with no underlying cash flow to fall back on.
examples: Investing is buying a claim on future earnings; speculation is buying a claim on someone else's future enthusiasm.
There's nothing wrong with speculating with money you can lose — the danger is doing it while calling it investing.
Most of what performs well on finance TikTok is speculation content, which is a real tension for anyone trying to build trust.
conversation: Viewer: Is this investing or gambling?
You: Speculation. Nothing wrong with it using money you can lose — the danger is doing it while calling it investing.
entries.note: Naming the line honestly — rather than moralizing about it — is what separates a credible finance creator from a scold or a shill.

entries.definition: Borrowed money used to buy investments, with your existing holdings as collateral.
examples: Trading on margin means a 20% drop can wipe out 100% of your money, and the broker doesn't wait for your feelings to catch up.
A margin call is the broker demanding cash immediately or selling your position for you at the worst moment.
Margin turns volatility from something you sit through into something that can end you.
conversation: Friend: The app offered me margin.
You: Then a twenty percent drop can wipe out a hundred percent of your money, and the broker will not wait for your feelings to catch up.
entries.note: Distinct from margin in the business sense (profit per sale). In an investing script, always say “on margin” so the context is unambiguous.

entries.definition: Pieces of a single share, letting you invest a dollar amount rather than a whole-share amount.
examples: Fractional shares are why $20 can buy a slice of a $600 stock — the barrier to starting used to be the share price and now it isn't.
They're table stakes in this category now; nobody's downloading an app because it offers them.
Fractional access changed who could start investing far more than any product feature of the last decade.
conversation: Viewer: I only have twenty dollars.
You: Fractional shares. You buy twenty dollars of the company instead of one whole six hundred dollar share.
entries.note: Historically important, commercially unremarkable today. Good for a “how we got here” script, bad for a landing page headline.

entries.definition: To bet against something by borrowing shares, selling them, and hoping to buy them back cheaper.
examples: When you short a stock, your maximum gain is capped at 100% and your maximum loss isn't capped at all — that asymmetry is the whole story.
A short squeeze happens when a rising price forces short sellers to buy back in, which pushes the price up further.
Shorting is the finance concept most frequently explained badly in 30 seconds, which is precisely why explaining it well travels.
conversation: Viewer: Explain shorting in ten seconds.
You: You borrow shares, sell them, hope to buy back cheaper. Your maximum gain is a hundred percent. Your maximum loss is not capped at all.
entries.note: The unlimited-downside point is the non-negotiable part of any script here. Leaving it out isn't simplification, it's a mistake.

entries.definition: Everything you own, considered as one thing rather than as a list of separate bets.
examples: Judge the portfolio, not the position — one holding being down doesn't mean anything on its own.
People check individual stocks daily and their portfolio monthly, which is exactly backwards.
A portfolio has a job: getting you to a goal by a date, at a level of risk you can hold through.
conversation: Friend: This one is down twelve percent.
You: Judge the portfolio, not the position. People check single stocks daily and the portfolio monthly, which is exactly backwards.
entries.note: The portfolio-level view is the mental shift beginners find hardest, and it's the foundation for diversification, allocation, and rebalancing all at once.
